title: Mictlan: A Journey after Death
subtitle: A posthumous journey in Spence's Mexica chapter

journey.excerpt: The dead person is given over to the tests which precede entrance to the abode of the dead, the realm of Mictlan, and so that he may not have to meet the perils of the journey in a defenceless condition a sheaf of javelins is bestowed upon him. He first passes between two lofty peaks, which may fall and crush him if he cannot skilfully escape them. A terrible serpent then intercepts his path, and, if he succeeds in defeating this monster, the fierce alligator Xochitonal awaits him. Eight deserts and a corresponding number of mountains have then to be negotiated by the hapless spirit, and a whirlwind sharp as a sword, which cuts even through solid rocks, must be withstood. Accompanied by the shade of his favourite dog, the harassed ghost at length encounters
journey.note: Verbatim prose from Lewis Spence's early twentieth-century synthesis, not a direct translation of the Indigenous source material he discusses. Preserve its dated, colonial framing.

narrativeBlocks.title: The four-year road
narrativeBlocks.body: For the Mexica, most dead went to Mictlan — a nine-level underworld reached by a four-year journey downward. It is not a judgment: nearly everyone takes the road.

narrativeBlocks.title: The dog that ferries
narrativeBlocks.body: At the first river, the soul needs a red dog — the xoloitzcuintli — to carry it across. That is why dogs were buried with the dead: the ferryman is waiting.

narrativeBlocks.title: Nine trials down
narrativeBlocks.body: The soul passes clashing mountains, a wind of knives, rivers and deserts — each level stripping away another layer of attachment to the world above.

narrativeBlocks.title: The lord of death's palace
narrativeBlocks.body: At the deepest level, Mictlantecuhtli, lord of the dead, receives the soul into final rest — an extinction more than a paradise or a punishment.

narrativeBlocks.title: A different moral map
narrativeBlocks.body: Unlike the Greek judgment hall, Mictlan is not earned — it is a process every ordinary soul walks. In this cosmos, how you die matters more than how you lived.
